title: Judge biases and calibration
summary: LLM judges have measurable habits: they favour the first position, longer text and their own outputs. You defend with order swapping, references, a different judge family and, above all, calibration against labels from one accountable human expert, reported as true positive and true negative rates.
useIf: A judge score will gate a release or rank candidates, so its errors must be measured and bounded.
avoidIf: You only need a rough trend and the judge's absolute accuracy does not matter.

explain.md: Treat a judge as an instrument with known error. The 2023 MT-Bench study measured several habits, and newer judges are likely better, but the mechanisms remain.

explain.caption: Biases, evidence and defences
head: Bias
Evidence
Defence
Cost
rows: Consistency after swapping answer order: GPT-4 65.0%, GPT-3.5 46.2%, Claude-v1 23.8% with the default prompt. Reordering let Vicuna-13B beat ChatGPT on 66 of 80 queries [[r21]] [[r31]]
Judge twice with swapped order and count a win only if it holds both ways, or randomise order
A repetitive-list attack fooled Claude-v1 and GPT-3.5 91.3% of the time and GPT-4 8.7% [[r21]]
Control for length, grade against criteria, not length

GPT-4 won about 10% more often and Claude-v1 about 25% more on their own outputs, though the paper called it inconclusive. Judges can recognise their own text, and self-recognition tracks self-preference [[r32]]
Judge with a different model family
Red team your judge with perturbations

explain.md: A few-shot judge lifted GPT-4's swap consistency from 65.0% to 77.5% at about 4x prompt cost, so mitigation has a price [[r21]]. Proposed calibration schemes include multiple evidence, balanced position and human-in-the-loop calibration [[r31]].

Do not quote these numbers for your own judge: measure it. Two cheap probes work on any judge. A **swap test** runs each pair in both orders and counts how often the verdict flips, and a high flip rate means position is driving the result. A **padding test** adds filler to one answer and checks whether the verdict moves toward the longer text. Both are reasoning-based probes, not vendor features.

steps.title: Label
steps.md: One principal expert gives pass/fail plus a written critique on 50 to 100 cases.

steps.title: Judge
steps.md: Run the judge on the same cases with the draft prompt.

steps.title: Compare
steps.md: Build a confusion matrix. Report true positive and true negative rates.

steps.title: Fix
steps.md: Read the disagreements, edit the rubric or add examples, rerun.

steps.title: Freeze
steps.md: Pin judge model and prompt. Re-check on a held-out labelled set.

explain.md: With imbalanced classes, raw agreement misleads. If 95% of outputs pass, a judge that always says pass scores 95% agreement and a true negative rate of 0%. Hamel Husain recommends reporting true positive and true negative rates and reached over 90% agreement in three iterations on one example [[r16]]. EvalGen research names **criteria drift**: people need criteria to grade outputs, but grading outputs helps them define criteria, so expect to revise the rubric [[tr3]].

whereToUse: Before a judge score becomes a CI gate
When ranking models from the same vendor family as the judge
When switching judge model or prompt, to prove parity
In regulated settings where evaluation evidence must be defensible

use: A judge score will gate or rank
An expert can label a calibration set
avoid: Calibrating on rows you also tuned the prompt against
Treating 2023 bias numbers as current for your judge
flips: Pairwise ranking: swap order every time
Judge and generator share a family: add a different-family judge for the final call
Stakes high: use two judge families and human review of disagreements

pitfalls.symptom: The judge reports 92% agreement yet misses most bad outputs
pitfalls.cause: 90% of outputs pass, so agreement is dominated by the majority class
pitfalls.fix: Report true positive and true negative rates and oversample failures in the calibration set

pitfalls.symptom: Judge agreement fell after a provider update
pitfalls.cause: The judge model changed behind an alias, or the prompt drifted
pitfalls.fix: Pin the version, keep a frozen calibration set and re-run it on every change

pitfalls.symptom: Calibration looks perfect but production disagreement is high
pitfalls.cause: The prompt was tuned on the same cases used to report agreement
pitfalls.fix: Hold out a labelled set the prompt never saw

scenarios.title: Same vendor for generator and judge
scenarios.situation: A team has one approved model deployment and uses it for both generation and judging. They compare two prompt versions and one wins by 6 points. Budget allows one extra deployment.
unknowns: Do both candidates have similar style?
How large is the calibration set?
scenarios.question: How do you reduce self-preference risk?

options.name: Add a judge from a different family and require both to agree, with order swapping
options.why: A different family removes the shared-style advantage, and swapping removes position bias.
options.tradeoff: Second deployment, and disagreements need a tie-break rule.

options.name: Keep the same judge, lower temperature
options.why: Temperature does not remove a preference for one's own style.

options.name: Ask a human to review all 300 pairs
options.tradeoff: Slow and costly for a routine comparison.

flips.then: Use reference-guided criteria and human review of a sample.

scenarios.takeaway: Break shared-family preference with a different judge.

scenarios.title: High-stakes gate, small expert budget
scenarios.situation: An assistant gives guidance in a regulated domain. An expert can label 80 cases once, and the release gate must be defensible to an auditor.
unknowns: What is the pass rate in the labelled cases?
scenarios.question: How do you build a gate you can defend?

options.name: Expert pass/fail with critiques, judge calibrated on a train and a held-out split, TPR and TNR reported, versions pinned
options.why: It is auditable, measures the error that matters and avoids overfitting the prompt.
options.tradeoff: Expert time and a small held-out set that gives wide intervals.

options.name: Report raw agreement only
options.why: A majority-pass dataset makes the number meaningless.
options.tradeoff: Raw agreement is fine when classes are balanced.

options.name: A panel of three judges and no human labels
options.tradeoff: No evidence that the panel agrees with the expert.

flips.if: Failures are rare in labelled data
flips.then: Oversample failures so TNR has enough cases.

flips.if: The expert can label more cases later
flips.then: Grow the held-out set to tighten intervals.

scenarios.takeaway: Defensible means calibrated, held out and version pinned.

quiz.q: An expert labels 200 outputs: 180 pass, 20 fail. The judge says pass on 175 of the 180 passes and fail on 8 of the 20 fails. What is the judge's true negative rate (fails caught), in percent?
quiz.hint: Caught fails divided by all true fails.
quiz.explain: 8 / 20 = 40%. Raw agreement is (175 + 8) / 200 = 91.5%, which looks good and hides that most bad outputs slip through.

quiz.q: A pairwise judge picks the first-listed answer 70% of the time on random pairs. What is the cheapest valid fix?
options: Judge both orders and count a win only if it holds both ways
quiz.explain: Swapping order and requiring agreement cancels position preference at the price of twice the calls. Temperature and rubric length do not address position, and always using the second position only flips the bias.

quiz.q: Which are reasons to calibrate a judge on a held-out labelled set rather than the set used to tune the prompt? Select all that apply.
options: The prompt can overfit the tuning cases
It gives an honest estimate of true positive and negative rates
It reveals drift after a judge model update
quiz.explain: Held-out data guards against overfitting, gives honest rates and exposes drift when rerun. It does not remove position bias, which needs order swapping.

flashcards.front: Why is raw agreement misleading for judges?
flashcards.back: With imbalanced classes it is dominated by the majority. If 95% pass, an always-pass judge has 95% agreement and a 0% true negative rate. Report TPR and TNR.

flashcards.front: How do you fix position bias in pairwise judging?
flashcards.back: Judge both orders and count a win only if it holds both ways, or randomise order. Cost is about double the calls.
A judge favouring its own model family's outputs. MT-Bench saw about 10% (GPT-4) and 25% (Claude-v1) higher win rates but called it inconclusive. Use a different judge family.
